claims.claim: Equity is the owners' claim on the business: the value that remains after subtracting what is owed from what is owned. OpenStax's Principles of Accounting states that equity is the value of an item that remains after considering what is owed for that item, and CFI states that equity is the value attributable to the owners of a business; the lesson uses both, attributed.

In the accounting equation, equity is the remainder: the equation assets = liabilities + equity rearranges to equity = assets − liabilities. OpenStax 2.2 demonstrates the equation with a home-loan example ($200,000 = $175,000 + $25,000), and CFI states the equation can be rearranged to equity = assets − liabilities.

Equity changes for four reasons: investments by owners increase it, net income (profits) increases it, distributions to owners (withdrawals) decrease it, and net loss decreases it. OpenStax 2.1 states that investments by owners and distributions to owners increase and decrease the value of the organization respectively, and that net income increases it while net loss decreases it; OpenStax 2.2 adds that organizations become more valuable through owner investments and profit and less valuable through distributions and loss.

Equity and liabilities are both claims on the business's assets, but liabilities are fixed outsider claims (banks, suppliers) while equity is the owners' residual claim. OpenStax 2.2 presents the sources-and-claims view: every asset has a claim against it, by creditors and/or owners; assets were obtained by incurring liabilities or were provided by owners.

Corporate equity has two broad parts: contributed capital (money owners put in, appearing as common stock in a corporation) and retained earnings (profit kept in the business — cumulative net income not distributed as dividends). OpenStax 3.2 states the expanded accounting equation considers contributed capital and retained earnings individually; OpenStax 2.2 states that income not distributed as dividends accumulates to form retained earnings and net losses decrease it; CFI states the sum of share capital and retained earnings equals equity.

The concept of equity does not change with the legal structure of the business, but the labels do: sole proprietorships use owner's capital and withdrawals (drawings), partnerships use partner capital accounts, and corporations use stockholders' equity with common stock and retained earnings, calling owner payouts dividends. OpenStax 2.1 and 2.2 state this terminology change across sole proprietorship, partnership, and corporation.

Equity is the balancing piece of the accounting equation and absorbs the risk of the business: because it is defined as the remainder after liabilities, a fall in asset values reduces the owners' claim first, before outsiders' claims are affected. This is the lesson's synthesized framing derived from the residual definition (CFI: equity = assets − liabilities) and the sources-and-claims view (OpenStax 2.2).

In investing, equity means ownership: a share of stock signifies an ownership position (called equity) in a corporation and a claim on its proportional share of the corporation's assets and profits, per the SEC's Investor.gov glossary.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources frame equity from two angles: OpenStax emphasizes the residual ('the value of an item that remains after considering what is owed'), CFI emphasizes ownership ('the value attributable to the owners of a business'), and Investor.gov emphasizes the investing sense (stock as an ownership position called equity).
positions: OpenStax Principles of Accounting, Volume 1, Section 2.1: equity is the value that remains after considering what is owed.
CFI Equity: equity is the value attributable to the owners of a business; book value equals assets minus liabilities.
Investor.gov glossary: a share of stock signifies an ownership position (called equity) in a corporation.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reconciles the two angles as one idea: equity is the owners' residual claim — the ownership angle and the remainder angle are two views of the same number, and the investing sense applies to shareholders in corporations. No factual conflict remains.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The parts of corporate equity are named differently across sources: OpenStax 3.2 names common stock and dividends as the equity elements of the expanded equation, while CFI names share capital and retained earnings.
positions: OpenStax 3.2: the expanded equation breaks equity into common stock, dividends, revenues, and expenses, considering contributed capital and retained earnings individually.
CFI Equity: the sum of share capital and retained earnings is equal to equity.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the standard broad labels contributed capital and retained earnings, noting that in a corporation contributed capital appears as common stock; the wording of the lesson and questions follows the broad labels to stay at literacy level.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-2 machine-generated draft for this topic is generic boilerplate (equity as a 'foundational concept in Accounting', a toolbox-drawer analogy, and definition-recite learning objectives); none of its claims were carried into the lesson, and no wording from it was reused.
correctionsNeeded: The working definition was verified against the live OpenStax Principles of Accounting Volume 1 pages (Sections 2.1 and 2.2) and the live CFI Equity page on 2026-08-21; the lesson's definition and equation statements reflect those verified sources.
The 'equity absorbs the risk' framing is labeled INTERPRETIVE in the evidence packet because it is the lesson's synthesis from the residual definition, not a quoted source statement.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified directly from the live OpenStax page on 2026-08-21. sourceRecords.title: Equity
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B (reputable secondary). Verified directly via live HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: equity as 'the value attributable to the owners of a business'; book value of equity as the difference between assets and liabilities on the balance sheet; the balance sheet equation rearranged to equity = assets − liabilities; the account also called shareholders'/owners'/stockholders' equity or net worth; accountants tracking share capital and retained earnings, where retained earnings consist of cumulative net income minus cumulative dividends and the sum of share capital and retained earnings equals equity; personal equity as net worth.
